title: Kinetic Theory of Gases
short_intro: The kinetic theory of gases models macroscopic thermodynamic properties of gases by considering microscopic random translational motion of constituent molecules. It establishes the mechanical origin of pressure and temperature in terms of molecular collisions.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Postulates of kinetic theory, pressure of an ideal gas, root-mean-square, average, and most probable speeds, concept of temperature, degrees of freedom, and law of equipartition of energy.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution function, mean free path, collision frequency, transport phenomena (viscosity, thermal conduction, diffusion), and real gas corrections via Van der Waals equation.

prerequisites: Concept of mole and Avogadro constant
Vector resolution and mechanics of elastic collisions

concept_notes.heading: Postulates of the Kinetic Theory of Gases
bullets: A gas consists of a very large number of identical, rigid, spherical molecules moving in random directions with all possible speeds.
The actual volume occupied by the gas molecules is negligible compared to the total volume of the container.
Molecules undergo perfectly elastic collisions with each other and with the walls of the container, conserving both total momentum and kinetic energy.

concept_notes.heading: Pressure of an Ideal Gas
bullets: Gas pressure arises due to the continuous bombardment of molecules against the walls of the vessel, resulting in a change of momentum.
The expression for pressure is P = (1/3)mnv<sub>rms</sub><sup>2</sup>, where m is mass per molecule, n is numerical density, and v<sub>rms</sub> is root mean square velocity.
Pressure depends only on the mass density and the mean square speed of the gas molecules, independent of the container shape.

concept_notes.heading: Degrees of Freedom and Equipartition of Energy
bullets: Degrees of freedom (f) represent the independent coordinates required to specify the dynamical state of a mechanical system.
Monoatomic, diatomic, and polyatomic gases possess 3, 5, and 6 degrees of freedom respectively at room temperature, with vibrational modes becoming active at high temperatures.

The Law of Equipartition of Energy states that in thermal equilibrium, the total kinetic energy of a dynamical system is distributed equally among all active degrees of freedom, each contributing (1/2)k<sub>B</sub>T per molecule.

concept_notes.heading: Maxwell-Boltzmann Velocity Distribution
bullets: The distribution function provides the probability fraction of molecules having speeds between v and v + dv at temperature T.
It yields three characteristic speeds: most probable speed (v<sub>mp</sub>), average speed (v<sub>avg</sub>), and root-mean-square speed (v<sub>rms</sub>).
The relationship between these characteristic speeds is always v<sub>mp</sub> < v<sub>avg</sub> < v<sub>rms</sub>.

derivations.title: Pressure Exerted by an Ideal Gas
derivations.conditions: N identical molecules of mass m inside a cubical container of side L.
steps: Consider a molecule moving with velocity component v<sub>x</sub> colliding elastically with a wall perpendicular to the x-axis at x = L.
The change in momentum during one collision with the wall is Δp<sub>x</sub> = -mv<sub>x</sub> - (mv<sub>x</sub>) = -2mv<sub>x</sub>.

The time interval between successive collisions with the same wall is Δt = 2L / v<sub>x</sub>, giving a collision force F<sub>x</sub> = (2mv<sub>x</sub>) / (2L / v<sub>x</sub>) = mv<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup> / L.
Summing over all N molecules and dividing by the area L<sup>2</sup> gives total pressure P = (m / L<sup>3</sup>) Σ v<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup>.

Using v<sub>rms</sub><sup>2</sup> = v<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup> + v<sub>y</sub><sup>2</sup> + v<sub>z</sub><sup>2</sup> = 3v<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup>, we arrive at P = (1/3)nmv<sub>rms</sub><sup>2</sup>.

derivations.title: Mean Free Path of Gas Molecules
derivations.conditions: Rigid spherical molecules of diameter d and number density n.
steps: A molecule of diameter d sweeps out a cylindrical volume of cross-sectional area πd<sup>2</sup> in moving with average speed v over time t.
The number of molecules swept through in time t is n(πd<sup>2</sup>v)t.
The average distance between successive collisions, known as the mean free path (λ), is the total distance traveled divided by the number of collisions.
Accounting for the relative velocities of colliding molecules introduces a correction factor of 1 / &sqrt;2.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Maxwell-Boltzmann Speed Distribution Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A skewed bell-shaped curve of fraction of molecules versus speed v, showing peaks for different temperatures T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub> (T<sub>2</sub> > T<sub>1</sub>).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: As temperature increases, the peak shifts to the right (higher most probable speed) and broadens, showing a wider range of molecular speeds.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in matching curves or identifying relative magnitudes of v<sub>mp</sub>, v<sub>avg</sub>, and v<sub>rms</sub>.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Pressure vs Temperature (Constant Volume)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin when extrapolated backward, intersecting the temperature axis at absolute zero (-273.15 °C).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates Gay-Lussac's law and confirms that pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature, vanishing at absolute zero.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to test the definition of absolute zero temperature.

graphs_and_experiments.title: PV/RT vs P Isotherms for Real vs Ideal Gases
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A horizontal straight line for ideal gas (Z=1) and curves showing significant deviations at high pressures for real gases.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the compressibility factor Z as a function of pressure, highlighting intermolecular forces and volume corrections.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: PGT questions on compressibility factor behavior at various pressure and temperature regimes.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the root-mean-square speed of hydrogen molecules at 300 K. Given the molar mass of hydrogen is 2 x 10<sup>-3</sup> kg/mol and R = 8.314 J/(mol K).
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: T = 300 K, M = 2 x 10<sup>-3</sup> kg/mol, R = 8.314 J/(mol K).
Substitute values: v<sub>rms</sub> = sqrt((3 x 8.314 x 300) / (2 x 10<sup>-3</sup>)).

solved_numericals.question: At what temperature is the root-mean-square speed of oxygen molecules equal to 1000 m/s? Molar mass of oxygen is 32 g/mol.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: v<sub>rms</sub> = 1000 m/s, M = 32 x 10<sup>-3</sup> kg/mol, R = 8.314 J/(mol K).
Rearrange rms speed formula to solve for temperature: T = (v<sub>rms</sub><sup>2</sup> M) / (3R).
Substitute values: T = ((1000)<sup>2</sup> x 32 x 10<sup>-3</sup>) / (3 x 8.314).

solved_numericals.question: Find the total internal energy of 2 moles of an ideal monoatomic gas at 27 °C. (R = 8.31 J/mol K)
solution_steps: Identify parameters: n = 2 moles, T = 27 °C = 300 K, monoatomic gas implies f = 3.
Use internal energy formula: U = (f / 2) nRT.
Substitute values: U = (3 / 2) x 2 x 8.31 x 300.
Simplify expression: U = 3 x 8.31 x 300 = 7479 J.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Intermolecular forces are completely neglected except during elastic collisions. Limitation: Fails at high pressures and low temperatures where real gas intermolecular attractive forces become significant.
Assumption: Volume of molecules is point-like compared to container volume. Limitation: Fails at high densities where the excluded volume correction cannot be ignored.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Temperature is a measure of the total kinetic energy of all molecules in a container.
common_misconceptions.correct: Temperature is a measure of the average translational kinetic energy per molecule.
common_misconceptions.why: Total kinetic energy depends on the total number of moles or molecules, whereas temperature is an intensive property reflecting mean kinetic energy per degree of freedom.

common_misconceptions.wrong: RMS speed and average speed of gas molecules are identical.
common_misconceptions.correct: v<sub>rms</sub> is always greater than v<sub>avg</sub>.
common_misconceptions.why: Root-mean-square speed weighs higher speeds more heavily since it is based on the square root of mean squared speeds.

quick_revision: Pressure P = (1/3) ρ v<sub>rms</sub><sup>2</sup> establishes the link between macroscopic pressure and microscopic motion.
Degrees of freedom determine the specific heat ratio gamma via Mayer's relation and equipartition theorem.
Characteristic speeds follow the fixed order: v<sub>mp</sub> < v<sub>avg</sub> < v<sub>rms</sub>.
